paras: The threatened lynching of Lemuel Ogden took place in March 1888 in Prince George's County, Maryland, when neighbors of the Fowler family talked of lynching Ogden, a white man charged with assaulting his sister-in-law, and tried to organize a party to visit the Marlboro' jail. No attack on the jail was reported, and Ogden was tried in April, found guilty and sentenced to 18 years in the penitentiary.

Ogden, described as thirty-five years old with a wife and four children, lived near Four Corners in Montgomery County, while his wife's family lived on the Bladensburg road about five miles from Washington. According to the account Catherine Fowler gave, he spent the evening of Monday, March 19, at her mother's house, entered her room about midnight, covered her mouth and threatened her, and assaulted her. She told her family after he left the next morning and obtained a warrant from Justice Hurley.

Sheriff Darnall found Ogden on Wednesday evening near McCeney's farm playing cards, though two other Washington papers put the arrest on Thursday. At a hearing before Justice Hurley, Fowler testified, and the justice stopped Ogden from contradicting her, saying any statement could be made in court. The sheriff then took the prisoner by train to Marlboro' and lodged him in jail.

By that time, the Evening Star reported, there had been "serious talk" among the Fowlers' neighbors about lynching Ogden, and after the sheriff left an attempt was made to organize a party to visit the jail. The coverage does not say whether the party formed or how many took part, and no later report mentions a crowd at the jail.

From jail, in a dispatch dated March 25, Ogden denied any assault and said he had gone home openly and made no attempt to escape. His trial opened at Upper Marlboro' on April 12 before Judges Brooke and Crane in a crowded courtroom, with State Senator Peter of Montgomery County among his counsel. On the stand Ogden said he had "accomplished his purpose" and claimed relations with Fowler since 1885, which she denied, and the jury returned a guilty verdict that evening.

In late June Judge Brooke sentenced him to 18 years in the penitentiary, declining to impose death in respect to a request for clemency from the family of Ogden's wife. The Montgomery County Sentinel reported that the case would be appealed to the Court of Appeals.

Washington papers framed the case as an "outrage," with headlines such as "ARRESTED FOR AN OUTRAGE" in the Evening Star and "HOSPITALITY OUTRAGED" in the Washington Critic. Only the Evening Star's fuller account of March 24 mentioned the lynching talk, in a single sentence without comment, and the Montgomery County Sentinel reprinted that account almost word for word a week later alongside Ogden's denial. The Critic and the National Republican did not mention it.

Beyond the region, wire notices carried only the guilty verdict, and the Rock Island Argus in Illinois headed its item "Give Him the Extreme Penalty." No Black-press coverage is available for this period.

bases: Neighbors of the Fowler family talked of lynching Ogden and tried to organize a party to visit the Marlboro' jail where he was held, but no attack on the jail is reported (A2, A5).

Ogden was not harmed: the papers report only lynching talk and an attempt to organize a party to visit the jail, and he was later tried, convicted and sentenced to 18 years (A2, A7, A15). The size of the would-be party is not given.

The lynching talk appears only in the Evening Star's account of March 24 (A2), which the Montgomery County Sentinel reprinted nearly word for word (A5); the other arrest reports do not mention it (A1, A3, A4).

accounts.label: Ogden's version (Upper Marlboro' dispatch)
accounts.gist: In jail Ogden denied any assault, said he stayed until 9 a.m., returned for a bundle, went home and made no attempt to escape.

accounts.label: Ogden's trial testimony

framing.detail: The Evening Star and Sentinel reported the lynching talk in one sentence of a narrative built on Fowler's account, neither endorsing nor condemning it.
Distant papers ran only the guilty verdict, the Rock Island Argus under 'Give Him the Extreme Penalty.'

conflicts.note: The accounts agree on the night of Monday March 19 into Tuesday March 20; 'Tuesday morning' is the early hours.
The Star's fuller account has arrest Wednesday evening and commitment Thursday.
Trial and sentencing reports use Lemuel R. W. Ogden.
'Hyattstown' in the March 25 dispatch is likely a slip for Hyattsville.
